summary: Defines IMAP extensions that improve international support, including language negotiation for error text, translations of namespace prefixes, and comparator negotiation for search, sort, and thread. IMAP4rev1 already handled non-ASCII mailbox names and MIME-encoded content in a basic way. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This lets an email program choose a language for messages and compare words in ways that fit different languages.

questions: how does imap comparator command work
subtitle: IMAP extensions for choosing the language of server messages and the rules used to search and sort text.

tldr.problem: IMAP4rev1 limits server response text to US-ASCII and matches search text case-insensitively, which serves non-English users poorly for error messages, folder names, and searching or sorting.
tldr.mechanism: A LANGUAGE command lets the client pick the language of server text and receive translated namespace prefixes, while I18NLEVEL=1 and I18NLEVEL=2 bring comparators to SEARCH, SORT and THREAD, with a COMPARATOR command at level 2.
tldr.outcome: It is a Standards Track extension that servers advertise as LANGUAGE, I18NLEVEL=1 or I18NLEVEL=2 in their capabilities, and the RFC says all servers should eventually comply with I18NLEVEL=2.

today: RFC 5255 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text says that legacy servers should advertise I18NLEVEL=1 and that all servers should eventually comply with I18NLEVEL=2.

sections.title: What the Extensions Add
sections.content:
IMAP4rev1 already has basic support for non-ASCII characters in mailbox names and search substrings, and for non-ASCII headers and content encoded with MIME. RFC 5255 defines two extensions of IMAP4rev1 that improve international support. They can be advertised and implemented separately.

The LANGUAGE extension lets the client request a suitable language for protocol error messages and, together with the NAMESPACE extension (RFC 2342), translated namespace names. The I18NLEVEL=2 extension lets the client request a collation that changes how SEARCH, SORT and THREAD behave, using the registry of RFC 4790. I18NLEVEL=1 is a simpler version that fixes the comparator to i;unicode-casemap (RFC 5051) with no choice.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two helpers. One makes the mail server speak your language. The other makes searching and sorting fair for words from your language.

sections.title: The LANGUAGE Command
sections.content:
Human-readable server text is limited to US-ASCII by the base IMAP specification, to stay compatible with deployed software. A server that supports this extension MUST list LANGUAGE in its CAPABILITY response and in the greeting, MUST use i-default until a language is negotiated, MUST include i-default among its languages, and MUST also support NAMESPACE. It SHOULD NOT advertise LANGUAGE if it only supports i-default.

The command is valid in all states. Clients SHOULD send it before authentication, because some servers send useful information such as an expired password during authentication. The client gives optional language ranges matched as in RFC 4647. On success the server answers in the first supported language, in UTF-8, and sends a LANGUAGE response; the change takes effect right after it. On failure the server keeps its previous language. The special argument default asks for the language the server administrator prefers.

With no arguments, the server SHOULD list its supported languages in one untagged LANGUAGE response. A response with a single tag means that language is now in use; a response with several tags is only a list and changes nothing.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the server which languages you speak, in order. It picks the first one it knows and switches. If it knows none, it keeps talking the way it was.

sections.title: Translated Namespace Prefixes
sections.content:
When localized names for namespace prefixes exist in the selected language, the server SHOULD add them to the NAMESPACE response using a TRANSLATION extension. It holds one string, the translation of the prefix in modified UTF-7. The client must convert between the real prefix and its translation when showing mailbox names to the user.

In the RFC's example, switching to German returns "Andere Benutzer/" for the prefix "Other Users/" and "Gemeinsame Postfächer/" for "Public Folders/", written in the RFC in modified UTF-7 as Ben&APw-tzer and Postf&AM8-cher. The extension changes only fixed server strings such as response text and namespace folder names. Localized aliases for shared mailboxes would need a separate mechanism, such as the proposed METADATA extension.
sections.plainLanguage: A folder called Public Folders can show up as its German name for a German speaker, while the computer still uses the original name behind the scenes.

sections.title: I18NLEVEL=1 and I18NLEVEL=2
sections.content:
The default comparator is what SEARCH and SORT use before any negotiation; the active comparator is the one in use in a session. It applies to the SEARCH keys BCC, BODY, CC, FROM, SUBJECT, TEXT, TO and HEADER, to the SORT keys CC, FROM, SUBJECT and TO if SORT is advertised, and to the subject comparisons in the ORDEREDSUBJECT and REFERENCES threading algorithms. A server advertising either level MUST implement i;unicode-casemap and MUST support UTF-8 as a SEARCH charset.

I18NLEVEL=2 is a superset of level 1. It adds the COMPARATOR command to see or change the active comparator, and the COMPARATOR response. A level 2 server MAY implement other comparators from the IANA registry and SHOULD use i;unicode-casemap as default; the default MAY depend on the user but MUST stay fixed once the connection is authenticated. Servers list the capability once in the authenticated state, and MAY list it earlier.

Because SEARCH needs the substring operation and SORT needs ordering (which needs equality), a server can only use collations that provide the operations its commands need. If the active collation lacks one, the server MUST respond with a tagged BAD. The RFC also notes that some earlier servers behave like level 1 without saying so, and others use i;ascii-casemap, so clients cannot know which comparator they get.
sections.plainLanguage: Level 1 is a fixed rulebook for comparing words. Level 2 lets you pick the rulebook that fits your language.

sections.title: Comparators and Character Encodings
sections.content:
The active comparator replaces the case-insensitive substring match in RFC 3501. A server does collation in steps. First, MIME encoding MUST be removed from the texts. Then the decoded text MUST be converted to the charset the active comparator expects.

For substring matching, if the conversion fails, the decoded text is compared using the i;octet comparator; if it succeeds, the active comparator is used. For ordering, strings that converted well are separated from those that failed. Good strings are validated and sorted with the active comparator, failed ones are sorted with i;octet, and the failed ones are appended after the rest. In the RFC's worked example of four Russian-looking strings, two are rejected as invalid UTF-8, and the final order is (4) (2) (3) (1). Strings in unknown or invalid encodings SHOULD be collated together.

If the substring operation of the active comparator returns the "undefined" result, the operation is repeated with i;octet. If MIME decoding fails for a message, collation of that message is implementation-dependent.
sections.plainLanguage: The server first unwraps the words, then turns them into one alphabet, then compares them. Words it cannot read go in a pile at the end.

sections.title: Other Internationalization Issues
sections.content:
The RFC lists issues it does not solve and leaves to other work, such as the EAI working group. The userid and password of the IMAP LOGIN command stay restricted to US-ASCII until a future standards track RFC says otherwise, and servers MAY reject a LOGIN containing an octet with the high bit set. With AUTHENTICATE, some servers may support Unicode userids and passwords because SASL allows it, but such userids cannot be used in email addresses.

The modified UTF-7 naming of RFC 3501 is described as a transition from earlier unofficial use of local character sets, and servers are encouraged to enforce its rules. On IDNA and MIME header conversion by servers, the RFC says it would be unwise to move forward before the work on international email addresses is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: Some things, like using any language in usernames and passwords, were left for later, so this document only makes a start.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
LANGUAGE is a new command in the Not Authenticated state. Some IMAP implementations run with root privilege in that state and are especially exposed to buffer overflows, so they need extra care parsing it.

A LANGUAGE command sent before a security layer is active can be attacked to suppress or modify the negotiation, which makes STARTTLS or authentication error messages harder to interpret. Clients MUST re-issue LANGUAGE once a security layer such as SASL or TLS is active. The extensions use UTF-8, so the security considerations of RFC 3629 apply, but identifiers do not use UTF-8, so the most serious concerns do not apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky person could mess up the language choice before the connection is locked. So you ask again once it is locked.
